## 7.1 Output and input streams
An *OutputStream* is a class that supports output. OutputStream provides several overloaded methods for writing a sequence of bytes to a destination. Usually placed into a buffer and then outputs the buffer at various times.
*System.out* is a predefined OutputStream object reference that is associated with a system' standard output, usually a computer screen.
The System class' out variable is a reference derived from OutputStream called a *PrintStream* (declared as `PrintStream out;` in the System class)

An *InputStream* is a class for achieving input data (keyboard, touchscreen, etc).
*System.in* is a predefined input stream object reference that is associated with a system's standard input, which is usually a keyboard.

A *byte stream* is used by programs to input or output 8-bits (a byte).
	System.in is an input byte stream, and this the read() method reads the first 8-bit ASCII value in the OS's buffer. These are turned as an int instead of byte. If the data is not available, return -1.

When using InputStream, you must append `throws IOException` to the definition of main()
A *throws clause* tells the JVM that the corresponding method may exit unexpectedly due to an *exception*.

The Scanner class augments an InputStream by automatically scanning a sequence of bytes and converting those bytes to the desired data type
## 7.2 Output formatting

Output formatting is adjusting the way that a program's output appears.

Typically using `printf()` and `format()` in System.out. Both methods are equivalent so we're only using printf().

The first argument of the printf() method, the format string, specifies the format of the text to print along with any number of placeholders for printing numeric values. These placeholders are format specifiers. Ot specifies the type of value to print in its place.

Format specifier begins with % followed by another character that indicates the value type to be printed.

%d indicates an integer, %s indicates a string,

![](data:image/png;base64,)

![](data:image/png;base64,)

A sub-specifier provides formatting options for a specifier and are included between the % and format specifier character.

printf("%.1f", myFloat); causes the floating-point variable to output with only 1 decimal digit.

![](data:image/png;base64,)

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Note: for width, periods count as characters

Note: for width, not truncated means it will print the whole number and not cut it off

Note: This works on strings not just numbers

NOTE: for the e thing, move the decimal to the left one space. Put all the existing decimals in (if no limit is specified), add a 0 at the end, then do e+01

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Printing strings is time-consuming and resource intensive. The processor resources are usually reserved and the system waits until the buffer is full, or reaches a certain threshold before outputting them. Or, with fewer characters in the buffer, the system may wait until resources are not busy.

If you do not want the system to wait. The PrintStream method flush() flushes the stream's buffer contents. Most Java implementations make System.out flush when a newline character is output or println() method is called.

System.out.flush();
#printf
## 7.4 File input
`fileByteStream = new FileInputStream(str);` creates a file input stream and opens the file denoted by a String variable, str, for reading. Can also pass a string literal.
